01.note: A heretic taunted Rabbi Yehuda that his plump, ruddy face looked like that of a moneylender or a pig breeder, people who grew rich without effort. Rabbi Yehuda answered that both trades are forbidden to Jews. His healthy color, he said, came from something else: there were twenty-four bathrooms between his home and the study hall, and he went into every one of them each time.
01.why: The Gemara is gathering anecdotes about Rabbi Yehuda's ruddy complexion: a teacher's remark about beets, a lady's accusation of drunkenness, and now a heretic's jibe, each answered with a different explanation.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose ruddy face draws remarks from several people in this run of stories.

terms.meaning: The Gemara's word for someone, often hostile to the Sages, who rejects their teachings; such figures often appear trading barbs with rabbis.

02.note: Rabbi Yehuda's wife gathered wool and made a thick cloak. She wore it when she went to the market, and he wore it when he went out to pray, reciting a blessing over it: "Blessed is He who wrapped me in a coat." Once, when Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel declared a public fast, Rabbi Yehuda stayed away, and people said it was because he had nothing decent to wear. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel sent him a cloak, but he refused it. He lifted the mat he sat on and told the messenger to look; in the translation's explanation, the space was miraculously full of gold coins. He said he simply did not wish to benefit from this world.
02.why: The Gemara has been telling a string of incidents from Rabbi Yehuda's life; right before this it shows him carrying his own seat to the study hall, saying labor brings honor. This story continues the theme of his poverty.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who lived in poverty, sharing a single cloak with his wife.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the community, who decreed a fast and sent Rabbi Yehuda a cloak.

terms.meaning: The president or head of the Jewish community and its Sages in the Land of Israel.
Public fasts were declared in times of trouble, such as drought; the community gathered together to pray.

03.note: Rabbi Akiva became engaged to the daughter of the rich bar Kalba Savua, who vowed she would get no benefit from his property. She married Rabbi Akiva anyway. They were so poor they slept on straw, and he said that if he could he would give her a golden crown. Elijah the prophet came disguised as a poor man begging straw for his wife in childbirth, and Rabbi Akiva said: see, he does not even have straw. She sent him to study Torah. After twelve years he came home, overheard a wicked man mocking her and her reply that she would gladly have him study twelve more, and turned back. He returned with 24,000 pairs of students. When the Sages pushed her away, he said his Torah and theirs was hers. Bar Kalba Savua then had his vow dissolved.
03.why: The Gemara has just told of Rabbi Yehuda, a poor scholar who could have been rich; this story continues the theme of poor scholars who become wealthy, and the Gemara goes on to list how Rabbi Akiva grew rich.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A poor man who becomes a great teacher after years of study, encouraged by his wife.

people.name: bar Kalba Savua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's wealthy father-in-law, who vowed his daughter could not benefit from his property.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as a poor man asking for straw.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's teachers.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's teachers.

terms.meaning: A spoken oath that makes something forbidden. A father could vow that his daughter would get no benefit from his property; a Sage could later dissolve such a vow if it was made under a mistaken assumption.
A golden crown or ornament, apparently shaped like the city of Jerusalem.

04.note: The Gemara lists six sources of Rabbi Akiva's wealth. One was his father-in-law Kalba Savua. Another was the carved ram on a ship's bow, used to hide money, which sailors once forgot on the shore and Rabbi Akiva found. Once he gave sailors four dinars to bring him something; all they found was a log on the seashore, and it turned out to be full of coins hidden there when a ship sank. The rest came from a convoy of Ishmaelites, from a certain lady, from the wife of Turnus Rufus and from Ketia bar Shalom; the translation explains, for instance, that the lady forgave a loan for which Rabbi Akiva had named God as guarantor.
04.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Akiva, once desperately poor, rose to fame and won back his father-in-law; it now adds how the poor scholar became rich, and goes on to a similar story about Rav Gamda.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A great Sage, once poor, whose sources of wealth are listed here.

people.name: Kalba Savua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's father-in-law, who had vowed his daughter would not benefit from his property.

people.name: Turnus Rufus
people.about: A Roman official whose wife is named as one source of Rabbi Akiva's wealth.

people.name: Ketia bar Shalom
people.about: Described in the translation as a Roman minister who left his fortune to Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of the period.
A carved figure of a sheep placed on a ship's bow, which, the translation explains, was used to hide money.

05.note: Rav Gamda gave sailors four dinars to bring him something from their travels. They found nothing worth buying, so they brought him a monkey. The monkey escaped and ran into a hole, and when they dug after it they found it crouching on pearls. They brought all the pearls to Rav Gamda.
05.why: The Gemara has just listed how Rabbi Akiva became wealthy, including from a log that sailors bought him for four dinars which turned out to be full of coins; this is a parallel tale of a lucky windfall.

people.name: Rav Gamda
people.about: A Sage who sends sailors to buy him something and ends up with pearls.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of the period.

06.note: The emperor's daughter told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, an unattractive man, that he was magnificent Torah in an ugly vessel. He asked her what her father's house kept its wine in. Earthenware jars, she said. He told her that ordinary people use earthenware, and royalty should use silver and gold. She moved the wine into silver and gold vessels, and it spoiled. He told her the same is true of Torah. When she asked whether there are not handsome people who are also learned, he answered that if they were ugly, they would be even more learned.
06.why: The Gemara has been telling stories about poor scholars; this exchange makes a related point, that a Sage's unimpressive outward vessel is no measure of the Torah inside him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage, described in the translation as unattractive, who answers the emperor's daughter.

people.name: the daughter of the emperor
people.about: A Roman princess who mocks Rabbi Yehoshua's looks.

terms.meaning: Here, the learning and wisdom of Jewish teaching that a scholar carries.

07.note: A man gave a friend his slave to be taught a thousand kinds of fig compote; the friend taught only eight hundred, and the man sued before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who marveled that he had never seen such plenty. Later Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held a lavish wedding for his son but did not invite bar Kappara. Bar Kappara remarked that if those who defy God's will are rewarded so richly, those who do it must get far more. He was invited, and said that if the righteous get this much in this world, they will get far more in the World-to-Come. Because calamity came on days Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi laughed, he promised bar Kappara forty se'a of wheat not to make him laugh. Bar Kappara put a huge tarred basket on his head and came to collect, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi laughed.
07.why: The Gemara has just explained a mishna's ruling by defining a kind of fig used for compote; the compote case follows from that, and the Gemara then moves to other incidents involving Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the wealthy head of the Sages, who judges the compote case and hosts his son's wedding.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A witty Sage who is left off the wedding guest list and later makes Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi laugh.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose wedding is described.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume for grain, roughly a few gallons.
The life after this one, where the righteous receive their full reward.
Ten thousand.

07.flag: The opening segment (the man who sues over a slave taught only 800 kinds of fig compote) is a separate incident from the bar Kappara stories that follow.

08.note: Bar Kappara told the daughter of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that tomorrow he would drink wine to her father's dancing and her mother's singing. Her husband, ben Elasa, a very rich man, was invited to the wedding of Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. There bar Kappara asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi the meaning of words the Torah uses for forbidden sexual acts, refuted every answer, and then offered his own explanation only once Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's wife had poured him wine and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had got up and danced for him. This happened three times. Ben Elasa could not bear to see his father-in-law humiliated, and he and his wife got up and left the wedding.
08.why: The Gemara is telling a run of incidents between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and bar Kappara around this same wedding; afterwards it turns to ben Elasa, explaining where else he is mentioned.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A witty Sage who makes good on his boast by getting Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to dance for him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the head of the Sages, hosting his son's wedding.

people.name: ben Elasa
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son-in-law, a very wealthy man.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose wedding this is.

terms.meaning: Hebrew words in Leviticus 18, translated abomination, perversion and lewdness. Bar Kappara explains each by a wordplay on its sound.
A common Talmudic way of referring to God as the author of the Torah.

09.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalls that Rabbi Tarfon once forbade him to eat even eggs that had been cooked together with meat he had vowed not to eat. The Rabbis answered that this is right only when the vow named a specific piece of meat: when a food someone has vowed off is mixed into another food and its taste can be detected, the mixture is forbidden too.
09.why: The Gemara is asking whether a vow on a food also forbids the juice that comes out of it. It cites this incident to show that naming a specific food extends the vow to what comes out of it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who tells of a ruling he received from Rabbi Tarfon.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who forbade Rabbi Yehuda eggs cooked with meat.

terms.meaning: A spoken declaration that makes a food or other thing forbidden to the person who says it, as binding as a religious law.
The rule that a forbidden food mixed into a permitted one makes the whole mixture forbidden if its taste can be detected.

10.note: The son of Master Shmuel ordered that Rava be given thirteen thousand dinars from the alalta, the crop, of his fields. Rava asked Rav Yosef what alalta includes. Rav Yosef said only the five grains; Abaye objected that it means everything that grows. Rava then said that was not his question: he wanted to know whether rent from houses and boats counts as a crop. Rav Yosef was angry that Rava had bothered him. On the eve of Yom Kippur Rava came to make peace, took the cup from the attendant and mixed Rav Yosef's wine himself, and the blind Rav Yosef recognized his way of diluting it. Rav Yosef told him not to sit until he explained a verse, and Rava taught that whoever makes himself humble like a wilderness receives the Torah as a gift and is raised up, while the arrogant are brought low.
10.why: The Mishna discusses vows on grain, and the Gemara has just ruled that the word for grain covers only the five species. This gift turns on whether a similar word, alalta, is equally narrow.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage to whom a bequest is made; he asks Rav Yosef a question and later makes peace with him.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Rava's teacher, who is blind and is angered by Rava's question.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rav Yosef's answer.

people.name: the son of Master Shmuel
people.about: A man who directs that Rava receive thirteen thousand dinars from his crop.

terms.meaning: Wheat, barley, spelt, oats and rye: the grains that count as grain in Jewish law.
Wine was strong and was normally mixed with water before drinking; each person had his own proportion.
The Day of Atonement; on its eve it is customary to make peace with anyone one has wronged.

11.note: A man found Rabbi Tarfon eating figs from his field at the end of the harvest, when the knives had mostly been put away. He put Rabbi Tarfon in a sack, lifted him up and carried him off to throw him into the river. Rabbi Tarfon cried out, "Woe to Tarfon, for this man is killing him!" Hearing who he was, the man dropped him and ran away. Rabbi Abbahu reports in the name of Rabbi Hananya ben Gamliel that all his life Rabbi Tarfon grieved over this, saying, "Woe is me, for I made use of the crown of Torah."
11.why: The Gemara has taught that once most harvest knives are put away, leftover figs are ownerless and may be eaten. Rabbi Tarfon was eating lawfully; the Gemara then explains that the owner took him for a thief and that he regretted escaping through his Torah status rather than his wealth.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage seized by a field owner while eating figs, who later regretted how he escaped.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage who reports Rabbi Tarfon's lifelong regret.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rabbi Abbahu reports the tradition.

terms.term: most of the knives have been set aside
terms.meaning: The end of the fig harvest, when cutting tools are packed away; what is left in the field is then treated as abandoned.
The honor due to a Torah scholar. Using it for personal gain was considered a serious wrong.

12.note: A man had vowed to get no benefit from his sister's daughter, not wishing to marry her, and Rabbi Yishmael took her into his house and made her beautiful. A teaching adds a detail: she had a false tooth, and Rabbi Yishmael made her a gold tooth with his own money. When Rabbi Yishmael died, a eulogizer began: "Daughters of Israel, weep for Rabbi Yishmael, who clothed you."
12.why: The Mishna rules that such a vow may be dissolved when the woman turns out to be beautiful, citing Rabbi Yishmael's case; this teaching fills in how he beautified her and how he was remembered.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who beautified a poor young woman at his own expense so that her uncle would marry her.

terms.meaning: A speaker who delivers the funeral address in praise of the dead.
A spoken declaration forbidding something to oneself. A Sage could dissolve it if it was made on a mistaken assumption.

13.note: A man vowed that his wife could get no benefit from him until she had given Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon a taste of her cooking; the translation explains that he wanted them to see how badly she cooked. Rabbi Yehuda tasted it. He reasoned that if the Torah lets God's holy name be blotted out in the sota ritual to make peace between husband and wife, even when peace is not certain, he could surely give up his dignity. Rabbi Shimon refused to taste it. He said: let all the widow's children die, and Shimon will not move from his place; and besides, people must not get used to making vows.
13.why: The Gemara is telling stories of vows that seem hard to keep or undo, and how Sages responded; this one sets two Sages' opposite answers to the same husband's vow side by side.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who tastes the wife's cooking to keep the peace in her marriage.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage who refuses, to protect scholars' dignity and to discourage vows.

terms.meaning: A word used to make a vow: declaring something konam makes it forbidden, as if it were consecrated to the Temple.
An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if this is true here, it is all the more true there.
In the sota ritual, a woman suspected of adultery drank water into which a written curse, including God's name, had been dissolved.

14.note: A man vowed that his wife could get no benefit from him until she had spat on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. She went and spat on his clothing. Rav Aha of Difti asked Ravina whether that was enough, since the husband had meant to humiliate Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel himself. Ravina answered that spit on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's clothing is a great humiliation, so the condition was met.
14.why: The Gemara is gathering cases of husbands who made their wives' benefit conditional on strange acts toward Sages; just before, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon split over whether a Sage should give up his dignity to save such a marriage.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The leading Sage whom a husband demanded his wife spit on.

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: A later Sage who asks whether spitting on the clothing fulfilled the vow.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who answers that it did.

terms.meaning: A word used to make a vow: declaring something konam makes it forbidden, as if it were consecrated to the Temple.

15.note: One man vowed that his wife could get no benefit from him until she had spat on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; she spat on his clothing, and Ravina held that this was humiliation enough to fulfil the vow. Another man vowed that his wife could get no benefit from him until she showed something beautiful about herself to Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei. He went through her head, hair, eyes, ears, nose, lips, neck, stomach and feet, and his students found fault with every one. Finally he asked her name: Likhlukhit. He said the name fit her beautifully, since she was dirty with blemishes, and so he permitted her to her husband.
15.why: Both cases follow a run of husbands' vows that made a wife's benefit depend on an act toward a Sage. Each shows a Sage finding a way to meet the condition so the couple could stay together.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The leading Sage whom one husband demanded his wife spit on.

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: A Sage who questions whether spitting on the clothing was enough.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who rules that it was.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who searches for something beautiful about a woman so her husband's vow can be met.

people.name: Likhlukhit
people.about: The wife in the second case, whose name becomes the one fitting thing about her.

terms.meaning: A word used to make a vow: declaring something konam makes it forbidden, as if it were consecrated to the Temple.
The woman's name, which sounds like a Hebrew word for dirty or stained; Rabbi Yishmael's wordplay turns on this.

15.flag: Two separate incidents (spitting on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and the search for something beautiful in Likhlukhit) are joined as one story.

16.note: A Babylonian moved to the Land of Israel and married a local woman, who took his Babylonian Aramaic too literally. Asked to cook "two lentils" (meaning a few), she cooked exactly two, and he was angry. The next day he asked for a se'a, meaning a lot, and she cooked a whole se'a. He asked for two butzinei, meaning small gourds, and she brought two lamps, the word's meaning in her dialect. In anger he told her to break them on the bava, meaning the gate. Bava ben Buta, a Sage, was sitting as a judge at the gate, and she broke the lamps on his head. When he asked why, she said her husband had told her to. He blessed her: since she had done her husband's will, may God give her two sons like Bava ben Buta.
16.why: The Gemara has been telling stories of husbands' angry demands on their wives and Sages who respond with forbearance; this one ends a run of such tales before the next Mishna turns to who may cancel a betrothed woman's vows.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: A Sage judging at the gate, on whose head the woman breaks the lamps; he blesses her.

terms.meaning: A large measure of volume, several gallons; the husband used it to mean simply a lot.
A name for God, meaning the One who is everywhere.
The Land of Israel, whose Aramaic dialect differed from the Babylonian one.

17.note: Isi bar Yehuda stayed away from Rabbi Yosei's academy for three days. Rabbi Yosei's son Vardimus found him and asked why. Isi answered that he could not come when he did not understand the reasoning behind one of Rabbi Yosei's teachings: that people's own laundry comes before the lives of others. What verse supports this? Vardimus offered to try to explain. The story stops with Isi's question and does not give Vardimus's answer.
17.why: The Gemara has been discussing how much laundering clothes matters, and returns to that topic here; the teaching Isi asks about ranks a town's own laundry above others' lives.

people.name: Isi bar Yehuda
people.about: A student who skips Rabbi Yosei's academy because he cannot understand one of his rulings.

people.name: Vardimus
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yosei, who seeks out Isi and offers to explain his father's reasoning.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Head of the academy, whose teaching on laundry puzzles Isi.

terms.meaning: A house of study where a Sage taught his students.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of their rulings.

17.flag: The story stops at Isi's question; Vardimus's answer is in the next segment, outside the story.

18.note: A man vowed that if he married before he had learned the law, all benefit from the world would be forbidden to him. He worked as hard as a man running up a ladder and a rope, but could not learn it. Rav Aha bar Rav Huna came and misled him, letting him think the vow would not take effect, and the man married. Then Rav Aha bar Rav Huna smeared him with clay, since clothing was now forbidden to him, and brought him before Rav Hisda to have the vow dissolved. Rava praised the plan, saying only a great man like Rav Aha bar Rav Huna would be wise enough to think of it.
18.why: Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis disagree about whether a vow that has not yet taken effect can be cancelled. Rava explains that Rav Aha let the vow take effect first because he held that the same dispute applies to having a Sage dissolve a vow.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who tricks the man into marrying so his vow can take effect and then be dissolved.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage before whom the man is brought to have his vow dissolved.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who praises Rav Aha bar Rav Huna's plan and explains it.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: An earlier Sage whose dispute with the Rabbis over cancelling vows Rava refers to.

terms.meaning: A Sage can release a person from a vow, usually by finding that he would not have made it had he foreseen the outcome.
A husband's power to cancel certain vows his wife makes, as distinct from a Sage's dissolving of a vow.
Jewish law, the practical rulings of the Sages.

19.note: A woman made a habit of rising early to wash her husband's hands on mornings after they had been intimate. One day she brought him the water, and he told her nothing had happened between them that night. She answered that in that case, perhaps it had been one of the gentile aloe merchants who had just been staying there. The case came before Rav Nahman, who said she may have set her eyes on another man, so there is no substance to her words.
19.why: The Gemara has been asking when a wife is believed about claims that would forbid her to her husband. Here her hint of adultery, which would have ended the marriage, is dismissed as unreliable.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who rules that the woman's claim is not to be believed.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew.
Traders in aloes, a fragrant wood or spice, apparently passing through and lodging nearby.

20.note: A woman was upset with her husband, and when he asked what had changed, she said he had never hurt her during intimacy the way he just had. He answered that nothing had happened between them just then. She said that in that case, perhaps it had been one of the gentile oil merchants who had been there. Rav Nahman said to those present: take no notice of her; she has set her eyes on another man.
20.why: The Gemara is asking when a wife is believed about claims that would forbid her to her husband; just before, Rav Nahman dismissed an almost identical claim by another woman, and this second case gets the same ruling.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who tells those present to ignore the woman's claim.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew.
Traders in oil, possibly naphtha or lamp oil, who had been staying nearby.
